case.answerKey: hold or restrict: observed availability is below the target
case.text: A fictional university communications gateway records 20 failed demands out of 10,000. It also records two outages in a 1,000-hour window, with one unavailable hour in total. The proposed availability target is 99.99%. The test assumes 10% external traffic; no new profile test is supplied.
case.lens: The gateway also relays the university's email. Its upgrade added a vendor's learned message classifier that flags phishing and routes messages. The vendor reports 98% accuracy on its own benchmark. In the pilot's 1,000 external messages, 50 were phishing. The classifier missed 10 and wrongly flagged 19 legitimate messages. Hold that question: after the measurement slides, one slide shows how this chapter's metrics and tests apply to the classifier.

glossary.short: a statement you say is true and can defend with evidence
the probability of failure-free operation over a stated time, in a given environment
the probability that the system is operational and can deliver service at a point in time
a system characteristic that can cause an erroneous state
the user-visible event when the service deviates from what is required
probability of failure on demand: failed demands divided by all demands
rate of occurrence of failures: failures divided by the time or transactions observed
mean time to failure: in this chapter, one divided by ROCOF
the count of demands or hours that a failure number is divided by
the input classes and how often each occurs in normal use
running the program on inputs that match real use, to measure reliability
a simpler, independent monitor that moves the process to a safe state
separate teams build versions of one specification; a voter compares their outputs
providing the same function in different ways so copies do not fail together
a table of what each message really was against what the classifier did
the inputs in use no longer match the inputs the model was trained and tested on

transfer.title: Transfer case · the textbook's bank ATM network
transfer.text: In the textbook's ATM example, a bank runs many cash machines. All of them use one customer account database. Database transaction mechanisms can correct problems in individual ATM transactions. This is a different system from the communications gateway.
transfer.source: Source slides 27–29 (ATM reliability and availability specification)
transfer.question: Which metric should the specification use for the shared account database service, and at what level?
transfer.answer: Availability, around 0.9999 between 7 am and 11 pm. If the database fails, every ATM stops, so availability matters more than reliability. Transaction mechanisms correct individual ATM errors, so a lower ATM availability of 0.999 is acceptable.
transfer.concept: matching the metric and level to the service
transfer.answerKey: availability of 0.9999 for the shared database

MAP.takeaway: Five source sections, five measurable outcomes, one decision with limits.

FAULT.answerKey: 24:xx state error; missed transmission is the failure
FAULT.commonError: Students answer “a bug” for all three terms. Have one student name the cause, one the state and one the lost service.

MANAGE.answerKey: analyzer detects; standby tolerates if service continues
MANAGE.commonError: Students treat a standby server as proof of fault tolerance. A design intention is not evidence that failover preserved the service.

RELAV.answerKey: B has less downtime: 60 minutes versus 360
RELAV.commonError: Students pick A because it fails less often. Ask them to compute total downtime, then ask who was affected and when.

METRICS.commonError: Students write 0.002 with no unit. Write the unit beside every number and separate outage events from failed requests.

lists.title: Reliability metrics
items: Probability of failure on demand
Rate of occurrence of failures, with mean time to failure as its reciprocal
Availability as a fraction of time

AVAIL.answerKey: 99.9 per cent: one lost hour in 1,000
AVAIL.commonError: Students switch between a 16-hour and a 24-hour window without saying so. Fix the service window before any arithmetic.

REQ.commonError: Students write “the system shall be reliable” as a requirement. Ask for a target and a mechanism as two separate sentences.
REQ.answerKey2: functional recovery requirement; the availability target is missing
REQ.question2: “Store recoverable copies on separate servers” is which kind of requirement, and what target is still missing?
REQ.answer2: It is a functional recovery and redundancy requirement. It still needs a service-level target and verification conditions. For example, an explicit availability requirement, a service window and a recovery test. Copies alone do not establish the achieved target.

PROTECT.answerKey: identical copies share the software fault
PROTECT.commonError: Students trace the protection sensors and the control sensors as one path. Trace them separately and ask which service is deliberately stopped.

SELFCHECK.answerKey: a mismatch, not which channel is right
SELFCHECK.commonError: Students read the status line as the result line. The comparator reports disagreement; the architecture must decide what happens next.

VOTE.commonError: Students take a 2-to-1 vote as proof that 18 is correct. Ask whether two copies of the same misconception can agree.
VOTE.question: Outputs are 18, 18 and 24. What does majority voting select?
VOTE.answer: The voter selects 18. Late outputs must also be handled by the specified timing rule.
VOTE.question2: What fact would defeat the claim that 18 is correct?
VOTE.answer2: A common specification or algorithm fault could make both agreeing versions wrong. Agreement alone does not establish correctness.

DIVERSITY.concept: shared failures that diversity does not remove
DIVERSITY.answerKey: a wrong requirement survives every language
DIVERSITY.commonError: Students list languages as evidence of independence. Ask for a common-cause counterexample before allowing an independence claim.

CODE1.answerKey: a reasonableness check across the series
CODE1.commonError: Students insert try/catch or a retry and stop. Ask what happens after the timeout and which state can be safely restored.
CODE1.concept2: limiting loss from a silent external failure
CODE1.question: A sensor value passes a numeric type check but is implausible compared with its earlier readings. Which check is missing?
CODE1.answer: A reasonableness check using the expected relationship across the series. A range check may also be relevant. A valid range and representation alone do not show that the sequence is plausible.
CODE1.question2: A remote service never replies during a long task. Name two mechanisms that limit the resulting loss.
CODE1.answer2: An external-call timeout returns control so a defined failure action can run. A valid saved checkpoint allows work to restart without losing the whole long transaction. State what is saved and what action follows the timeout.

MEASURE.answerKey: a defect-hunting dataset distorts the input distribution
MEASURE.commonError: Students assume one test suite answers both “can I break it?” and “how often does service fail in use?”. Contrast the two purposes.

lists.title: Data needed to measure reliability
items: The number of failures for a number of service requests; this measures POFOD, whatever the time span
The time or transactions between failures plus the total elapsed time or transactions; this measures ROCOF and MTTF
The repair or restart time after a failure that loses service; this measures availability

PROFILE.answerKey: 700, 200 and 100; the estimate stays with its profile
PROFILE.commonError: Students read percentages off the source histogram. It has none; the 70/20/10 split is a labelled course calculation.
PROFILE.answer: 700, 200 and 100. If actual use shifts, update the class probabilities and the representative test dataset. The previous estimate stays limited to its previous profile.

LIMITS.commonError: Students invent a confidence interval or a certification rule from a zero-failure run. Keep the limitation visible beside the number.
LIMITS.answer: The profile, the exposure or sample size, the service and failure definition, the operating conditions and the statistical uncertainty. No observed failure in one limited test is not proof of zero future failure probability.

lists.title: Reliability measurement problems
items: Operational profile uncertainty: the profile may not reflect real use
High costs of test data generation when data cannot be generated automatically
Statistical uncertainty: highly reliable systems rarely fail, so significant failure counts are hard to get
Recognizing failure: a specification can be read in conflicting ways

AISYS.commonError: Students report 97.1% accuracy as the reliability. Accuracy averages over messages that are not protection demands and hides the misses.
bullets: The confusion matrix rows are what each message really was; its columns are what the classifier did.
How many demands support that estimate?
AISYS.takeaway: Ninety-seven per cent correct and still missing phishing: find the denominator that matters.
AISYS.question: Compute both numbers. Which one can support a protection claim, and what caveat do 50 demands require?
AISYS.answer: Accuracy = (40 + 931) / 1,000 = 97.1%. Phishing POFOD = 10 / 50 = 0.2 per phishing demand. False-alarm rate = 19 / 950 = 2.0%. Only the POFOD for the protection demand can support a protection claim. State it with its exposure (50 demands) and its profile (10% external traffic). Accuracy averages over messages that are not protection demands and hides the misses. With 50 demands the estimate is uncertain. A standard 95% interval for 10/50 runs from roughly 11% to 33%.

REVISE.answerKey: re-measure on the new profile before any protection claim
REVISE.commonError: Students keep the verdict and the old explanation. A student may keep the same verdict only with a new explanation of its scope.
bullets: External traffic rises from 10% to 60%; the classifier learned mostly internal mail.
The POFOD estimates belong to the old profile: explain what changes.
Restrict the release claim, re-measure on a representative mix, and name who accepts the restricted scope.
REVISE.answer: Revise the profile and the representative test dataset before transferring the old measured ratio to the new traffic mix. Keep the claim limited while testing. Name the decision owner and reviewer. Disclose AI use and verify any calculation or generated tests independently. Do not mark a proposed test as completed evidence. For the classifier, the profile change is also a distribution shift. Re-measure its phishing POFOD on a representative external mix before claiming protection. If protection is reduced meanwhile, tell the users whose mail it screens.

stations.answerKey: availability for the gateway; POFOD for the phishing demand
stations.think: Devices down. Hold, restrict or release, and which metric supports that scope?
stations.pair: Name one assumption and one given fact you need to support your answer.
stations.write: Write your claim and its evidence. Mark any test you only propose as proposed.
stations.hint: Name the service or property first. Use a source definition and the given facts. Ask which missing fact would change your claim. Decide which metric fits the classifier's phishing demand.
stations.note: Think without devices, then pair. Choosing when not to use technology is part of using it well. Use the same card; nobody is marked on field length or a timer.
stations.answer: An answer with limits separates the given facts from the needed evidence. The example gives POFOD 0.002 per demand, ROCOF 0.002 outages per hour and availability 99.9%. These describe different events and exposures. For the classifier, overall accuracy of 97.1% hides the protection demand. It missed 10 of 50 phishing messages: a POFOD of 0.2 per phishing demand, measured on only 50 demands.

criteria.name: Names the mechanism
levels: Names the chapter mechanism that decides the case and says how it applies.
Names a mechanism but does not connect it to the case facts.
No chapter mechanism, or the wrong one.

criteria.name: Uses only the given facts
levels: Every statement rests on a given fact or is marked as an assumption.
Mostly given facts, but one invented or unmarked assumption.
Relies on facts the case does not give.

criteria.name: Evidence another person can check
levels: Names evidence a second engineer could inspect, and marks proposed tests as proposed.
Names evidence, but it is vague or its status is unclear.
Opinion or confidence instead of evidence.

rubric.marks: 2 marks per criterion, 6 in total. Not graded in class. The same reasoning earns the assignment points.

strong.text: Hold full release. Availability is the metric for a continuous gateway: one lost hour in 1,000 is 99.9%, below the 99.99% target. For the classifier, the phishing POFOD is 10/50 = 0.2, on only 50 demands. A profile test under the real traffic mix is proposed.
strong.why: Names the right metric for each service, computes from the given numbers and marks the proposed test.

weak.text: Release: the vendor says 98% accurate and the servers were up almost all the time.
weak.why: Uses the vendor's benchmark instead of the given facts; no metric, no denominator, no test.

rubric.other: Other answers are accepted when they use a chapter mechanism and rest on the given facts. They must also name evidence someone else can check. A different decision with those three is as strong as the model answer.

stations.answerKey: a rule-based check fails for different reasons than the classifier
stations.think: Compare two mechanisms: an identical second server, or a second AI classifier as a diverse version. Which one would you choose?
stations.pair: Ask your partner to argue for the mechanism you rejected. Name one trade-off and one thing both mechanisms share.
stations.write: Write why your mechanism supports your claim, and what you are still unsure of.
stations.hint: Explain why the mechanism affects your claim. Then name a shared cause, a mismatch or a limit outside its evidence.
stations.answer: Tie the chosen mechanism to the required property. Say what the alternative improves or sacrifices. Evidence of a shared dependency or mismatched assumption can defeat an apparently stronger design. A second classifier trained on similar data may share the same blind spots. N-version teams can share a specification error in the same way. A rule-based check or human review is more likely to fail for different reasons. That too needs a reason you can state.

criteria.name: Links the mechanism to the property
levels: Explains how the chosen mechanism affects the property at stake.
Names the mechanism without the link to the property.

criteria.name: Names a shared cause or limit
levels: Names a specific shared cause, mismatch or limit that could defeat the mechanism.
Mentions a limit in general terms only.
Treats the mechanism as always enough.

criteria.name: States the trade-off
levels: Says what the alternative improves and what it costs.
Gives one side of the trade-off only.

rubric.marks: 2 marks per criterion, 6 in total. Not graded in class. The same reasoning earns the assignment points.

strong.text: Neither as given. A second identical server improves availability against hardware faults but shares every software fault. A second classifier trained on similar mail shares its blind spots. A rule-based check fails for different reasons, at the cost of more false alarms.
strong.why: Links each mechanism to its property, names the shared cause and states the trade-off.

weak.text: Add the second classifier: two AIs are better than one.
weak.why: No property named, no shared cause, no cost.

rubric.other: Other answers are accepted when they use a chapter mechanism and rest on the given facts. They must also name evidence someone else can check. A different decision with those three is as strong as the model answer.

stations.answerKey: the miss rate does not travel to the new traffic mix
stations.think: External traffic changes from the assumed 10% to 60%. No representative result under that mix is supplied. The classifier was trained mostly on internal messages. Does your first decision still hold?
stations.pair: Explain what changes in your claim, your evidence or its scope.
stations.write: Record the new evidence and your revised decision with its limits. Say plainly what your first card got wrong. Name the responsible role and who must be told.
stations.hint: Do not simply repeat your first answer. Name the changed assumption, the next evidence and the condition that would change your decision.
stations.note: Classroom version only. The assessed assignment has its own new evidence, revealed after you commit.
stations.answer: The new fact changes the stated assumption, so the original evidence cannot be widened silently. Retain, restrict or revise the decision with a reason, a new verification requirement and a named owner. The classifier's miss rate was measured on a mostly internal mix. Under 60% external traffic it faces inputs unlike its training data. Its phishing POFOD must be re-measured before any protection claim.

criteria.name: Says what the new fact changes
levels: Names the assumption the new fact breaks and what it leaves intact.
Notes the new fact without saying which assumption it breaks.
Ignores or restates the new fact.

criteria.name: Revises with a reason
levels: Keeps, changes or replaces the decision for a reason from the new fact. Says what the first answer got wrong.
Changes the decision without a clear reason, or hides the first answer.

criteria.name: Names the owner and who is told
levels: Names the role that decides and the people who must be informed.
Names neither the owner nor who is told.

rubric.marks: 2 marks per criterion, 6 in total. Not graded in class. The same reasoning earns the assignment points.

strong.text: My first card assumed the 10% external mix would hold; it will not. Revise: restrict the release to internal mail and re-measure the phishing POFOD on an external sample. The service owner decides; the mail users are told that screening is reduced.
strong.why: Names the broken assumption, revises with a reason, admits the first error, names owner and audience.

weak.text: Keep my decision; 0.2 was measured, so it still applies.
weak.why: Ignores the profile change; names nobody.

rubric.other: Other answers are accepted when they use a chapter mechanism and rest on the given facts. They must also name evidence someone else can check. A different decision with those three is as strong as the model answer.
